title: Dual-Calibration Compact Anchor Learning for Multi-View Clustering
one_liner: Learn a small set of anchors for each view, then force sample-to-anchor assignments and final cluster assignments to agree in both directions so the anchors become compact and semantically useful.
lead: Multi-view clustering groups the same objects using several feature views, such as text plus images or sensors from different modalities. Anchor methods speed this up by replacing all pairwise sample comparisons with comparisons to a smaller anchor set. The problem is that anchors are often chosen or learned in a way that covers the data broadly but does not line up cleanly with the actual cluster boundaries. This paper proposes dual calibration: use the anchor space to inform clustering, then use the emerging clusters to push back on the anchors so both spaces become mutually consistent.

problem.h2: Fast anchor clustering breaks when the anchors do not respect cluster semantics
paras: In multi-view clustering, each object appears in several feature spaces. Directly comparing every sample with every other sample is expensive on large datasets, so anchor-based methods introduce a smaller set of representative points. Each sample connects to anchors rather than to all other samples. This saves time because the method now stores and updates a small graph instead of the full sample graph, but the anchor set becomes the model's internal map of the data. If that map is blurry, clustering is blurry too.

Existing methods often initialize anchors by random sampling or constrain them with simple algebraic rules that spread them apart. That can reduce redundancy, but it does not guarantee that one anchor represents one coherent semantic region. Two anchors may cover the same cluster, or one anchor may sit across a cluster boundary. Then the sample-to-anchor assignments fail to reflect the true grouping structure, and the final clustering inherits that mistake.

callout.html: Anchor methods are only as good as the anchors, and broad coverage is not enough because clustering needs anchors that align with semantic boundaries.

steps.text: Each view gets a small anchor set that roughly covers where its observed samples lie.
For every view, each sample receives connection weights to a few nearby anchors instead of to all samples.
A clustering layer converts the anchor-based representation into shared cluster memberships across views.

steps.b: Calibrate anchor space from cluster space
steps.text: If a sample's cluster membership disagrees with its anchor neighborhood, the anchor assignments are updated to reduce that mismatch.

steps.b: Calibrate cluster space from anchor space
steps.text: If anchors from different views imply the same semantic grouping, cluster memberships are updated to respect that shared evidence.

paras: The paper changes anchor learning from a one-way preprocessing step into a bidirectional optimization loop. Earlier anchor methods largely treated anchors as fixed supports for later clustering. Here, anchor assignments and cluster assignments repeatedly correct each other. That matters because clustering semantics are not fully visible in the original sample space or in the anchor space alone; they appear when both spaces are forced into agreement.
object.object: the relationship between anchor learning and cluster assignment

hidden.name: cross-space consistency
paras: Cross-space consistency measures whether a sample is telling the same story in two internal languages: its anchor neighborhood and its final cluster assignment. If the sample attaches strongly to anchors that mostly represent cluster 2, but the clustering layer assigns it to cluster 5, the model is internally inconsistent.

The algorithm estimates this consistency during alternating optimization. It computes sample-to-anchor weights in each view and cluster memberships in the shared clustering space, then penalizes disagreement. As the penalty shrinks, anchors become less redundant and more discriminative because only anchors that support stable cluster structure survive repeated calibration.

cells: sample 1 with anchor group A and cluster A
heat.caption: Dark cells are cases where anchor assignments and cluster assignments agree strongly. Light cells mark ambiguity, redundancy, or cross-view disagreement that the calibration loop tries to remove.

reads.html: The model wants each sample's anchor neighborhood and cluster label to support the same grouping decision. When they do not, the model treats that as evidence that either the anchors or the cluster assignment is wrong.

Dual calibration aligns the anchor space and the clustering space through bidirectional consistency constraints, so anchor learning is directly supervised by the evolving clustering semantics rather than by coverage alone.

mechanism.h2: Why bidirectional calibration improves anchor quality
paras: Anchor quality depends on what the anchors are optimized to preserve. If they are optimized only for reconstruction or geometric spread, they can still ignore the actual cluster structure. Dual calibration adds the missing training signal: the anchor graph is good only when it produces cluster assignments that remain consistent across views, and the clusters are good only when they are supported by coherent anchor neighborhoods.

This mutual correction loop removes two common failure modes. First, redundant anchors are pushed apart functionally because if two anchors serve the same cluster region, the model gains nothing from keeping both and the calibration penalty favors a cleaner partition. Second, ambiguous boundary anchors are corrected because samples near a boundary receive cluster feedback showing that their anchor support should concentrate more on one side.

Alternating optimization matters because neither space is perfect at the start. Early anchors are noisy, and early cluster assignments are noisy. By passing information back and forth, the algorithm gradually builds anchors that are compact in coverage and discriminative in meaning, which is exactly the combination large-scale clustering needs.

stages.s: Multiple feature views of the same samples
Learn view-specific anchors and sample-to-anchor links
Infer shared cluster memberships from those links
Send cluster corrections back to anchor assignments
Compact anchors whose neighborhoods match cross-view cluster semantics

math.words: Each sample receives anchor weights in every view. A clustering layer maps those weights to cluster memberships. Training minimizes reconstruction or fitting terms together with a penalty that discourages disagreement between anchor-space structure and cluster-space structure.
math.equation: minimize over anchors and assignments: fitting_loss + lambda * cross_space_consistency_loss
symbols: the objective that keeps samples close to useful anchors in each view
the penalty for disagreement between anchor assignments and cluster assignments
the weight that controls how strongly the model enforces dual calibration

worked.title: A tiny worked example with two anchors and one disputed sample
lines: Suppose one sample in view 1 connects 60 percent to anchor A and 40 percent to anchor B. In view 2, the same sample connects 70 percent to anchor A and 30 percent to anchor B.
If the clustering layer still assigns that sample mostly to the cluster represented by anchor B, the consistency penalty is high because the two anchor views both lean toward anchor A.

During optimization, either the cluster membership shifts toward the anchor A cluster or the anchor weights move if the sample was linked badly. The update that reduces disagreement and keeps neighboring samples coherent is favored.
After several rounds, the sample should either become clearly attached to anchor A and its cluster or reveal that one of the anchor sets was misplaced.

math.note: The equation is short, but the important part is the feedback direction: the consistency term is not only checking the final clusters. It is also shaping which anchors are worth keeping.

bars.h2: What the method is trying to improve

charts.title: Anchor method without dual calibration
charts.note: Large-scale efficiency is preserved, but anchor redundancy and cluster ambiguity remain because the anchor set is not corrected by clustering semantics.

charts.title: Dual-calibrated anchor method
charts.note: The small loss in simplicity is exchanged for cleaner anchors because agreement with cluster assignments acts as direct supervision on anchor quality.

items.html: If the first anchors miss important regions badly, the early cluster assignments are also bad. Then both spaces may reinforce the same mistake because each is correcting toward a flawed partner.

If one view groups samples by one criterion and another view groups them by a different criterion, dual calibration can over-force agreement and hide real structure because the method assumes a shared clustering signal that should be preserved across views.

items.b: Too many anchors erase the benefit.
items.html: A very large anchor set reduces the need for compactness, so the model can keep redundant anchors and still fit the data. Calibration becomes weaker because there is less pressure to summarize cleanly.

Use enough anchors to cover the data but not so many that redundancy is free, initialize anchors near dense regions, and apply dual calibration only when the views should share cluster semantics. Then the anchor graph becomes both compact and discriminative.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Create a synthetic dataset with two views of the same points. In view 1, clusters are separated mainly by horizontal position. In view 2, they are separated mainly by vertical position plus noise. Run one anchor-based clustering method that learns anchors without feedback from clustering and one that adds a dual consistency penalty between anchor assignments and cluster memberships.
demo.metric_eq: cluster_accuracy = matched_correct_labels / total_samples; redundancy_rate = duplicate_or_unused_anchors / total_anchors
demo.closing: The demo should show two things at once: dual calibration lowers anchor redundancy and raises clustering accuracy because the anchor set is repeatedly corrected toward the cluster structure that both views support.
